discovery: Invention and development of the optical lattice atomic clock

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics (precision measurement, laser-cooled atoms)
motivation: Katori conceived the 'magic wavelength' optical lattice, which traps thousands of laser-cooled atoms without shifting their clock transition. This combines the long interrogation times of trapped ions with the statistical power of many atoms. Katori and Ye turned this idea into strontium and ytterbium clocks with fractional uncertainties near 10^-18, about a hundred times better than caesium standards. These clocks have resolved gravitational redshift over millimetre height differences, set new limits on any drift of the fundamental constants, opened relativistic geodesy, and probed many-body physics in atomic ensembles. They are leading the redefinition of the SI second. I helped build an atomic clock in Brazil, so I know how hard it is to reach this level of control. Their work grows directly out of laser cooling and trapping and has made precise timekeeping a tool for fundamental physics and a technology for society.
